newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France reopens Telecom sale dossier. [CORRECTED 13:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France reopens Telecom sale dossier. [CORRECTED 13:55 GMT]

text.p: France Telecom welcomed on Friday a government move indicating that the Socialist-led administration may revive a partial privatisation of the group which it suspended after coming to power last month.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin charged former labour minister Michel Delebarre on Thursday (correcting day) with consulting France Telecom's staff and management before the government decided on the possible partial privatisation of the group.
"We welcome the nomination of Michel Delebarre and France Telecom, chairman Michel Bon in particular, are at his disposal a company spokesman said.

Delebarre has to report back to the government before September 5. "The new government said it needed time to think things over. This appointment means that that things are moving," the spokesman added.

The mission allows Jospin to deliver on his election promise to consult France Telecom staff before taking a decision, and gives him time test the resistance against the sale by the three communist ministers in his cabinet.

The previous conservative government had been planning to bring about 35 percent to the market in the country's biggest ever International Public Offering (IPO). The company was estimated to be worth between 160 billion francs and 210 billion francs ($26-$35 billion).

The operation, initially scheduled for May, was postponed by a month after President Jacques Chirac called an early parliamentary election and suspended after the Socialist party formed a government with the communists and greens.
The Communist party is opposed to any privatisation.
Company chairman Bon is in favour of a partial privatisation to help France Telecom to face the competition in a liberalised French and European market from 1998.
A listing of France Telecom shares would also permit a share swap with ally Deutsche Telekom, already on the market.

The France Telecom spokesman reiterated the company's view that such a swap would help the Atlas alliance between the two telecom giants and that a listing was needed to establish the market value of the respective companies.
The Force Ouvriere union said it was pleased the government had "reopened the privatisation dossier of France Telecom".
Financial analysts said the appointment seemed to indicate the government was edging towards a sale.

"If they want to do it this year, they have to take account of STET, or Telecom Italia as it will be called. STET is coming to the market this autumn," said Richard Jones of Yamaichi. However, the Italian parliament still has to amend laws before the sale can go ahead.

"France Telecom, a public enterprise, must continue to assure the public service duties defined by the law...Within this framework, adaptations may prove necessary to benefit its European and international development and to preserve its leading place in an essential sector," a joint statement by the Finance and Industry ministries said.
Since taking office, the Socialists have said there could be sales of minority stakes in state companies which operate in a competitive market.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn is "not against" a partial sale. While privatisation revenues cannot be used to reduce the budget deficit to qualify for European monetary union, the money can be used to finance some operations that would otherwise have weighed on the deficit.
Other state-owned groups such as insurer GAN, bank Credit Lyonnais and railways group SNCF need cash.
France Telecom staff are divided on the issue of a sale.

The former government won over a lot of resistance by assuming the pension liabilities for France Telecom staff and by allowing current staff to keep their status as civil servant. Not all of France Telecom's 165,000 staff are civil servants.
The Communist-led CGT, the biggest union at France Telecom, fiercely opposes a sale and is organising a petition among staff against a privatisation. It has 13,000 signatures sofar.
But some unions including Force Ouvriere have said they would support a partial sale under certain conditions. ($ = 6.056 French Francs)
